title: Newcastle upon Tyne
wiki_lead:
Newcastle upon Tyne, or simply Newcastle (  new-KASS-əl, RP:   NEW-kah-səl), is a city and metropolitan borough, in Tyne and Wear, England. While the hyphenated form of the name, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, is seen sometimes, correct usage is generally unhyphenated.
It is England's northernmost city, sited on the river Tyne's northern bank opposite Gateshead to the south. It is the most populous settlement in the Tyneside conurbation and North East England. The metropolitan borough had an estimated population of 320,838 in 2025.
Newcastle developed around a Roman settlement called Pons Aelius. The settlement became known as Monkchester before taking on the name of a castle built in 1080 by William the Conqueror's eldest son, Robert Curthose. It was one of the world's largest ship building and repair centres during the Industrial Revolution. The city was historically part of the county of Northumberland, but governed as a county corporate after 1400. In 1974, Newcastle became part of the newly created metropolitan county of Tyne and Wear. The local authority is Newcastle City Council, which is a constituent member of the North East Combined Authority.

History


Roman era
The first recorded settlement in what is now Newcastle was Pons Aelius ("Aelian bridge"), a Roman fort and bridge across the Tyne. It was given the family name of the Roman emperor Hadrian, who founded it in the second century AD. This rare honour suggests Hadrian may have visited the site and instituted the bridge on his tour of Britain. The population of Pons Aelius then was estimated at 2,000. Fragments of Hadrian's Wall are visible in parts of Newcastle, particularly along the West Road. The course of the Roman wall can be traced eastwards to Segedunum, a Roman fort in Wallsend  and to the separate supply fort of Arbeia in South Shields, across the river from Hadrian's Wall.
The extent of Hadrian's Wall was 73 miles (117 km), spanning the width of Britain; it incorporated the Vallum, a large rearward ditch with parallel mounds, and was built primarily for defence and to prevent the incursion of Pictish tribes from the north. It was probably not as a fighting line for a major invasion; however, it seems that the Vallum stopped just west of Newcastle, where its role as a secondary line of defence was performed by the Tyne.


Anglo-Saxon and Norman eras

After the Roman departure from Britain, completed in 410, Newcastle became part of the powerful Anglo-Saxon kingdom of Northumbria and was known throughout this period as Munucceaster (sometimes modernised as Monkchester).
Conflicts with the Danes in 876 left the settlements along the river Tyne in ruins. After battles with the Danes and following the 1088 rebellion against the Normans, Monkchester was all but destroyed by Odo of Bayeux.

grok_lead: Newcastle upon Tyne is a city and metropolitan borough in Tyne and Wear, North East England, located on the northern bank of the River Tyne. Its name derives from a castle constructed in 1080 by Robert Curthose on the site of the Roman fort Pons Aelius, with the surviving stone keep built by Henry II between 1172 and 1177. As of the 2021 census, the population stood at approximately 300,000, reflecting a 7.1% increase from 2011. Historically a major industrial centre, Newcastle upon Tyne prospered through coal mining, shipbuilding, and engineering from the 18th to early 20th centuries, driving rapid population growth from 28,000 in 1820 to over 215,000 by the late 19th century. The city's economy has since transitioned toward services, education, and digital sectors, supported by institutions like Newcastle University and Northumbria University, which contribute to a vibrant student population and research output. Iconic landmarks include the Tyne Bridge, opened in 1928 and emblematic of the region's engineering heritage and modern identity. Newcastle upon Tyne is renowned for its cultural vibrancy, including a prominent nightlife, Geordie dialect, and events centred around Newcastle United Football Club, a fixture in English top-flight football. The city's quayside and Grey Street exemplify Georgian architecture amid post-industrial regeneration efforts that have revitalized former industrial zones into commercial and residential hubs.
